meta_title: Distribution Automation Software for Orders | VOS
meta_desc: Take the hand-work out of the order path. VOS is distribution automation software for one stretch of it: capture, approval, then delivery into your systems.
text: of hand-work removed from one order
running, with nobody staffing the inbox
is the whole setup for most food distributors
Six people touch an order before anything gets picked.
Nobody designed it this way. It accumulated. Three stretches of that journey still done entirely by hand:
Someone takes the call, scribbles the list, repeats it, then fixes whatever got misheard. Twenty minutes per customer.
The same lines go from a pad into a screen, matched to codes from memory, with one more chance to go wrong.
To confirm it, to query a quantity, or to say an item is out. Another call, another note, another gap.
What distribution automation software can take off your team
The order writes itself up as it is spoken.

Your customer works down their own account guide and the app builds the list as they go. Nobody on your side listens, writes, or reads anything back, because whoever knows the order is the one creating it.
No call to answer and no voicemail to clear
Lines matched to your codes as they are said
Each quantity attached to one of your SKUs
Works at 2am as well as at 2pm
A distribution automation system still needs a human yes.

The buyer reads the completed order and approves it before anything leaves their phone, then gets a confirmation when it lands. That is deliberate: distribution automation software that fires orders off without anyone looking just automates the mistakes.
Approval sits with the person who placed it
We never submit an order for somebody
Their confirmation arrives as an alert or a text
Interrupted halfway? Their place is held
Straight into your systems on a direct feed.

The last manual step on the path is somebody entering the order where it belongs. Choose EDI, QuickBooks or the API and that step is gone outright, which is the part of any distribution automation solution your office actually feels.
One delivery route, agreed at onboarding
Nothing gets keyed again on those routes
A file sent by email may still need keying on your side
Your ERP and invoicing carry on as they are
Each order files itself against the customer.

Reference number, time of sending and line items, kept beside the account that ordered. Nobody maintains a log, nobody updates a spreadsheet, and a question about last Tuesday is answered on a screen rather than in a conversation.
Its own reference on anything the app sends
Kept on one screen for your staff
Phone orders carry none of this, as before
Smaller jobs nobody counts until they stop appearing.
Send a promotion by a push or a text into the app, rather than working down a sheet of numbers.
A stock picture that moves with the ordering, drawn from the inventory tools you have.
A confirmation goes back on its own, so customers ring less often to ask whether it arrived.
Count the steps that would disappear
Walk us through the journey an order makes today, and we will show you what is left afterwards.
There is nothing to build, script or connect before you start. Three steps, and the manual stretch at the front is gone.
What they buy, at your figures, with your codes: one guide each. A spreadsheet each is fine.
Most distributors are switched on inside 24 to 48 hours. Nothing is installed on a machine of yours.
Spoken, approved and delivered by your chosen route. Most buyers send one the day they are set up.

Distribution automation software covers very different ground depending on who is selling it. VOS automates the run from a customer's decision to a record in your system. Trucks, warehouses and invoices are not on that list, and the table says so.
Removes the call from order intake
Arrives coded, no entry step on direct routes
The customer is told it arrived
Sends orders with no human involved
What gets automated, and what does not
Which parts does distribution automation software like this cover?

One stretch, end to end: a customer deciding what they need, the order being written up and approved, and the result landing in your systems coded, with its own reference. Everything after that, from picking to delivery to the invoice, belongs to the software you have.
Will it place orders for our customers automatically?

No, and that is a design decision rather than a missing feature. A person reads the lines and sends them. Nothing goes out on a customer's behalf, because an order sent by a machine on a bad assumption is a credit note with extra steps.
Can we really get rid of the retyping?

On the EDI, QuickBooks and API routes, yes: the record arrives in your system without anyone touching it. If you take orders as an emailed PDF, Excel or Word file instead, somebody may still key it in. That is the one choice in setting up distribution automation software worth thinking about properly.
Do we need middleware or a developer?
No. There is nothing to host, no script to write and no integration platform in the middle. We agree the delivery method with you during onboarding and it keeps working without maintenance.
Can the old way keep running alongside it?

Yes. Phone orders still get handled by a person, exactly as now, and they carry no reference or send time from us. The place to begin is your most frequent orderers, since that is where the hours pile up.
Is this automated software distribution, as in deploying software?

No. If you are looking for an automated software distribution tool to push applications and patches out to laptops and servers, that is a different field entirely. VOS has no part in it. We are about food orders moving from a restaurant to its distributor.
Does this relate to grid distribution automation?
Also no. In the electricity industry the same term covers feeder switching, fault location and outage management on a power network. Nothing here touches utilities. The overlap is only in the words.
How many accounts need to move for this to be worth doing?

Savings land per order, not per customer, so it turns on how often they order. Start with the handful of customers ordering most often. We quote for each distributor, so ask us to run through the arithmetic on the call.
